crew.kade.text: A launch window is more than a time on the clock. Check upper-level winds and lightning risks before choosing when to go. If conditions fall outside your limits, hold the launch.
crew.rios.text: A heavier payload leaves less room in your mass budget. Track mass and power margins as the design evolves. Test power, communications, and guidance together before declaring the vehicle ready.
crew.sol.text: Choose samples that can answer your mission question. Match your instruments to the material you expect to study. Leave enough time and power to analyze and transmit the results.
crew.vega.text: Start by defining one measurable mission objective. Set clear go/no-go criteria and decide who makes the final call. Protect time and budget for testing and contingencies.

lesson.architecture.text: Plan four connected segments: launch, space, ground, and users. Define how each one contributes to the mission objectives.

lesson.ground.text: Prepare Mission Control, communications, tracking, contingency procedures, launch criteria, and operating schedules.

lesson.systems.title: SYSTEMS ENGINEERING

flightData.orbit.LEO.name: Low Earth orbit (LEO)
flightData.orbit.LEO.plain: Roughly 200 to 2,000 km up. This is the easiest and least expensive orbit to reach. The International Space Station circles Earth about every 90 minutes.
flightData.orbit.LEO.examples: International Space Station, small telescopes, and satellite internet networks.
flightData.orbit.SSO.name: Sun-synchronous polar orbit (SSO)
flightData.orbit.SSO.plain: This near-polar orbit passes over a location at roughly the same local time, so images have similar lighting. It takes more fuel because the launch makes little use of Earth’s rotation.
flightData.orbit.SSO.examples: Landsat, PACE, and other Earth-observation satellites.
flightData.orbit.GTO.name: Geostationary transfer orbit (GTO)
flightData.orbit.GTO.plain: An elongated orbit reaching roughly 36,000 km above Earth. The spacecraft burns its own propellant to enter a geostationary orbit over the equator.
flightData.orbit.GTO.examples: GOES weather satellites and communications satellites.
flightData.orbit.TLI.name: Translunar injection (TLI)
flightData.orbit.TLI.plain: The spacecraft leaves Earth orbit on a trajectory toward the Moon, about 384,000 km away.
flightData.orbit.TLI.examples: Artemis I, CAPSTONE, and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.
flightData.orbit.ESCAPE.name: Escape from Earth
flightData.orbit.ESCAPE.plain: The spacecraft escapes Earth’s gravity on its way to a planet or asteroid. This destination takes the most fuel.
flightData.orbit.ESCAPE.examples: Europa Clipper, Psyche, Lucy, and Mars rovers.

flightData.fact.east.text: Rockets often launch east to gain speed from Earth’s rotation. At the equator the surface is already moving at about 1,670 km/h.
flightData.fact.east.source: Earth’s rotation: about 465 m/s at the equator.
flightData.fact.fuel.text: Most of a rocket’s liftoff mass is propellant. The spacecraft, the reason for going, accounts for only a small fraction.
flightData.fact.fuel.source: For Falcon 9, Ariane 6, and others, propellant exceeds 85% of liftoff mass.
flightData.fact.iss.text: The International Space Station travels about 28,000 km/h and orbits Earth every 90 minutes. Its crew sees about 16 sunrises per day.
flightData.fact.origami.text: Large satellites and telescopes travel folded inside the fairing and unfold once they reach space.
flightData.fact.origami.source: The James Webb Space Telescope unfolded during its journey.
flightData.event.weather.label: Weather delay
flightData.event.weather.explain: Every day on hold costs money because the crew, pad, and propellant remain committed. Sites with suitable weather can reduce this risk.
flightData.event.minorAnomaly.label: Countdown held after a false alarm
flightData.event.minorAnomaly.explain: A sensor showed an unexpected reading. An inspection costs time and money, but is safer than proceeding.
flightData.event.orbitOffset.label: A gust pushed the rocket off course
flightData.event.orbitOffset.explain: A high-altitude gust pushed the rocket. Without a correction, the spacecraft may spend some of its own propellant to recover the orbit.
flightData.event.failure.label: Rocket failure
flightData.event.failure.explain: No launch is completely risk-free. A good flight record matters for high-value missions.
flightData.event.engineOut.label: An engine lost power
flightData.event.engineOut.explain: An engine may shut down or deliver less thrust. The rocket can keep flying, but fuel must be managed carefully.
flightData.difficulty.facil.description: Fewer options and step-by-step help. The launch site and inclination are chosen automatically.
flightData.difficulty.facil.label: Easy
flightData.difficulty.normal.description: A larger catalog, weather events, and insertion errors. Schedule delays cost money.
flightData.difficulty.normal.label: Normal

flightData.glossary.carga-util.title: Payload capacity
flightData.glossary.carga-util.text: How much mass a rocket can carry. The same rocket can lift far more to low orbit than to a high orbit or the Moon.
flightData.glossary.carga-util.more: Payload capacity in the catalog depends on the destination. Values are rounded and simplified for the game.
flightData.glossary.delta-v.title: Delta-v budget
flightData.glossary.delta-v.text: How much a spacecraft must change its velocity. A typical launch to low Earth orbit needs around 9.4 km/s of delta-v, including losses.
flightData.glossary.delta-v.more: This estimate includes gravity and drag losses. See orbital-mechanics tables and NASA’s Basics of Space Flight.
flightData.glossary.delta-v.formula: Δv = exhaust velocity × ln(initial mass / final mass)
flightData.glossary.orbita-alta.title: Why does a higher orbit cost more?
flightData.glossary.orbita-alta.text: Each extra kilometer per second takes more propellant. That propellant adds mass too, so a rocket that carries 17 tons to low orbit might carry only 5 toward 36,000 km.
flightData.glossary.orbita-alta.more: Propellant requirements grow exponentially with delta-v in the rocket equation.
flightData.glossary.margen.title: Payload margin
flightData.glossary.margen.text: Unused rocket capacity after loading your spacecraft. Designs often get heavier as they mature. Green means comfortable, yellow tight, and red risky.
flightData.glossary.margen.more: Margin % = (capacity − spacecraft mass) ÷ capacity × 100. Thresholds depend on difficulty.
flightData.glossary.cofia.title: Payload fairing
flightData.glossary.cofia.text: The fairing protects the folded spacecraft from airflow and heating. When the air is thin enough, the fairing opens and separates.
flightData.glossary.cofia.more: Catalog dimensions are approximate usable sizes based on rocket user guides.
flightData.glossary.confiabilidad.title: How many launches out of 100 succeed?
flightData.glossary.confiabilidad.text: A rocket with 99% reliability still fails once in about 100 launches. For a one-off mission, an established flight record can be worth paying for.
flightData.glossary.confiabilidad.more: Public flight records inform the estimate. Reliability for new rockets is an approximation for the game.
flightData.glossary.inclinacion.title: Orbital inclination
flightData.glossary.inclinacion.text: An equatorial orbit is at 0° and a polar orbit is near 90°. Launching into a lower inclination than the site latitude needs an expensive plane change.
flightData.glossary.inclinacion.more: A change in orbital plane of Δi at speed v costs Δv = 2·v·sin(Δi/2).
flightData.glossary.ventana.title: Launch window
flightData.glossary.ventana.text: The time when the departure geometry works for your destination. For Mars, good opportunities recur about every 26 months.
flightData.glossary.ventana.more: 26 months is approximately the Earth–Mars synodic period.
flightData.glossary.rideshare.title: Rideshare
flightData.glossary.rideshare.text: Several spacecraft share a rocket and split the cost. It is cheaper, but the primary mission sets the date and exact orbit.
flightData.glossary.rideshare.more: Examples include SpaceX Transporter and Bandwagon. The catalog uses approximate published rates.
flightData.glossary.maxq.title: Maximum dynamic pressure (Max-Q)
flightData.glossary.maxq.text: About a minute after launch, the rocket is fast while the air is still dense. Rockets can briefly throttle down to reduce aerodynamic loads.
flightData.glossary.maxq.more: Dynamic pressure is q = ½·ρ·v². The game warns at 30 kPa and uses a 40 kPa limit.
flightData.glossary.gto.title: Geostationary transfer and orbit (GTO and GEO)
flightData.glossary.gto.text: At roughly 36,000 km, a satellite over the equator can appear stationary. A rocket typically leaves it in an elongated transfer orbit, then the spacecraft circularizes using its own fuel.
flightData.glossary.gto.more: GEO altitude is 35,786 km. A launch farther from the equator can increase the propellant cost of reaching it.
flightData.glossary.propelente.title: Loading less propellant
flightData.glossary.propelente.text: If the spacecraft is too heavy, carrying less propellant can make it fit. The trade-off is less fuel to maintain orbit and a shorter useful life.
flightData.glossary.propelente.more: In the game, useful life is proportional to remaining operational propellant.
flightData.glossary.trade.title: Trade study
flightData.glossary.trade.text: NASA engineers compare several designs before selecting one. An option may be cheaper, safer, or faster. Compare what you gain with what you give up.
flightData.glossary.trade.more: This comparison is called a trade study.
flightData.glossary.presupuesto.title: Budget
flightData.glossary.presupuesto.text: Launch is a major expense. Every million spent on the rocket is a million unavailable for instruments, testing, or operations.
flightData.glossary.presupuesto.more: Approximate catalog costs draw on public contracts and published prices.
flightData.glossary.apoapsis.title: Highest orbital point (apoapsis)
flightData.glossary.apoapsis.text: A spacecraft is farthest from Earth and moving most slowly at the highest point of an elongated orbit. This is a good place to burn to circularize.
flightData.glossary.apoapsis.more: Around Earth, the apoapsis is also called apogee.
flightData.glossary.periapsis.title: Lowest orbital point (periapsis)
flightData.glossary.periapsis.text: The lowest point is closest to Earth. Below about 150 km in the game, atmospheric drag means the spacecraft will eventually fall back.
flightData.glossary.periapsis.more: Around Earth, the periapsis is also called perigee.
flightData.glossary.gravity-turn.title: Gravity turn
flightData.glossary.gravity-turn.text: A rocket rises vertically to clear thick air, then gradually turns sideways. Getting to orbit requires sideways speed, not just altitude.
flightData.glossary.gravity-turn.more: Begin gently around 2 km of altitude in the game. Turning too sharply in dense air can break the rocket.
flightData.glossary.throttle.title: Thrust and throttle
flightData.glossary.throttle.text: Throttle sets how hard the engines push from 0 to 100%. Higher thrust accelerates faster but uses more propellant and increases aerodynamic loads.
flightData.glossary.throttle.more: Real engines have throttle and restart limits. The game simplifies these.
flightData.rocket.electron.summary: A small rocket for CubeSats and similar satellites. A dedicated flight lets you choose the orbit and date.
flightData.rocket.rideshare.summary: Your spacecraft flies with several others. The ride costs less, but the main mission chooses the orbit and date.
flightData.rocket.pegasus.summary: It launches from an aircraft in flight. It is expensive for its size, but it can launch close to the equator.
flightData.rocket.alpha.summary: An inexpensive rocket that can carry over a ton, with a shorter and riskier flight record.
flightData.rocket.pslv.summary: An economical Indian rocket widely used for Earth observation from polar orbits.
flightData.rocket.vegac.summary: A European rocket designed for polar orbits. It cannot reach very high orbits.
flightData.rocket.falcon9.summary: A frequently used rocket with a reusable first stage. Recovery reduces the maximum payload it can carry.
flightData.rocket.ariane64.summary: A heavy European rocket launched from near the equator in Kourou, an advantage for geostationary transfers.
flightData.rocket.falconheavy.summary: Three Falcon cores provide high thrust, but the payload fairing is the same size as Falcon 9’s.
flightData.rocket.sls.summary: The Artemis rocket. It is very large and expensive, useful for heavy payloads to the Moon or beyond.

flightData.reference.tropics.note: CubeSat constellation studying hurricanes, launched in pairs on small rockets.
flightData.reference.elana.note: NASA helps universities launch CubeSats as secondary payloads. See CubeSat 101.
flightData.reference.capstone.note: A 12U CubeSat that reached the lunar orbit planned for Gateway.
flightData.reference.trailblazer.note: A small lunar satellite that shared a launch with another mission.
flightData.reference.icon.note: Studies the ionosphere. Its target inclination was 27°, lower than Florida’s latitude, so it launched from an aircraft.
flightData.reference.ixpe.note: An X-ray telescope in an equatorial orbit. Changing the orbital plane by nearly 28° used much of the Falcon 9’s performance.
flightData.reference.tess.note: An exoplanet hunter in a high orbit influenced by the Moon’s gravity.
flightData.reference.pace.note: Observes oceans, aerosols, and clouds from a roughly 676 km Sun-synchronous orbit.
flightData.reference.lro.note: Has mapped the Moon since 2009. Shared a launch with LCROSS.
flightData.reference.swot.note: Measures Earth’s surface water from an 890 km orbit inclined 77.6°.
flightData.reference.landsat9.note: Images Earth from a 705 km Sun-synchronous orbit.
flightData.reference.psyche.note: Travels to the metal-rich asteroid Psyche on the first Falcon Heavy hired by NASA for planetary science.
flightData.reference.mars2020.note: Launched during the July–August 2020 Mars window. The next opportunity was 26 months later.
flightData.reference.clipper.note: NASA’s largest planetary spacecraft. Its Falcon Heavy launch did not recover the boosters.
flightData.reference.jwst.note: Launched from Kourou. The Ariane 5 insertion was so accurate that Webb saved propellant and gained years of useful life.
flightData.reference.artemis1.note: First SLS flight, taking an uncrewed Orion around the Moon.

flightData.fact.moonAim.text: The Moon is about 384,000 km away, and a spacecraft can take three to five days to get there. Aim for where the Moon will be on arrival, not where it is at launch.
flightData.fact.moonAim.source: Average Earth–Moon distance: 384,400 km. Apollo missions took about three days.
flightData.fact.reentry.text: A capsule returning from the Moon enters near 40,000 km/h. Its heat shield tolerates nearly 2,800 °C, and the parachutes slow it to about 30 km/h before splashdown.
flightData.fact.reentry.source: NASA Artemis I (2022): Orion entered at about 39,400 km/h, its heat shield reached about 2,760 °C, and it splashed down near 32 km/h.
